questions.title: Entity
questions.text: Which statement best defines an **entity**?

options.content: A single property such as a surname
A thing, person or event about which data is stored
A field that uniquely identifies a record
A link between two tables

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: An entity has its own data and many instances; it becomes a table. A single property is an attribute.

questions.title: Attribute
questions.text: *A cinema stores films, screenings and customers.* Which item is an **attribute**, not an entity?

options.content: Film
Screening
Customer
Running time

scheme.mark_scheme: D.
scheme.explanation: Running time is one value that describes a film, so it is a field of the Film table.

questions.title: Order of design
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

First the analyst identifies the [[1]] and their attributes from the requirements. Then the relationships are drawn in an [[2]]. Finally every field is described in the data [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) entities (2) ERD (3) dictionary

questions.title: Entity or attribute
questions.text:
*A car-rental company records customers, cars and rentals. For each car it stores the registration number, model and daily price.*

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

scheme.mark_scheme: Customer entity (1); Daily price attribute (1); Rental entity (1); Model attribute (1)
scheme.model_answer: Customer — entity; Daily price — attribute; Rental — entity; Model — attribute.
scheme.explanation: Customer and Rental have their own data and many instances; daily price and model are single values describing a car.

questions.title: Design documents
questions.text: Match each document or statement to what it contains.

right.text: The design built in the DBMS
The name, type, size, key and validation of every field
The tables and how they are related (1:1, 1:M)
What the client needs the system to store and report

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R4, L2–R3, L3–R2, L4–R1. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Choosing a primary key
questions.text: A music school stores `StudentID`, `FirstName`, `Surname`, `DateOfBirth` and `ParentPhone` for each student. Which field is the most suitable **primary key**?

options.content: Surname
DateOfBirth
StudentID
ParentPhone

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: A primary key must be unique, never empty and should not change. Surnames and birthdays repeat; a parent's phone can change or be shared by siblings.

questions.title: Degree of a relationship
questions.text: Match each pair of entities to the degree of the relationship between them.

left.text: Country — Capital city (each country has one capital)
Class — Pupil (a pupil is in one class)
Student — Elective course (students take several electives)

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R3, L3–R2. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Ask the question in both directions: a class has many pupils, but a pupil is in one class → 1:M.

questions.title: Where the foreign key goes
questions.text: One teacher teaches many lessons; each lesson has one teacher. Where is the foreign key `TeacherID` placed?

options.content: In the Teacher table
In the Lesson table
In both tables, as a primary key
In a new link table

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: The foreign key goes in the table on the "many" side of a 1:M relationship.

questions.title: Storing M:M
questions.text: A many-to-many relationship can be implemented directly by adding one foreign key to either of the two tables.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A field holds only one value, so one foreign key cannot list many partners. An M:M relationship is replaced by a link entity with two foreign keys.

questions.title: Name the link entity
questions.text: A school library: each member borrows many books, and each book is borrowed by many members over a year. State a suitable name for the **link entity** that resolves this many-to-many relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme: Loan
scheme.explanation: One record per borrowing — the Loan — holds MemberID and BookID as foreign keys, plus the dates.

questions.title: Degrees in a gym
questions.text:
*A gym: each training session is for one member with one trainer; members have many sessions; trainers run many sessions; a member may train with several trainers.*

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

scheme.model_answer: Member — Session — 1:M; Trainer — Session — 1:M; Member — Trainer — M:M.
scheme.explanation: Session is the link entity that resolves Member M:M Trainer into two 1:M relationships.

questions.title: Crow's foot
questions.text: In crow's foot notation, what does the crow's foot (three short lines) at one end of a relationship line show?

options.content: That entity is on the "one" side
That entity is on the "many" side
That entity has no primary key
The relationship is optional

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: The crow's foot touches the entity that has many records for one record of the other entity.

questions.title: Fields of a link entity
questions.text: The link entity **Loan** resolves Member M:M Book. Select the **three** fields that Loan should contain.

options.content: LoanID (primary key)
MemberID (foreign key)
MemberName
BookID (foreign key)
BookTitle

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Names and titles are already stored in Member and Book; repeating them in Loan would be redundant.

questions.title: Why design first
questions.text: Select **two** reasons why the database is designed (ERD and data dictionary) **before** the tables are built.

options.content: Errors are found on paper before data is entered
The tables no longer need primary keys
Programmers build tables whose keys and types fit together
Validation is no longer needed

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Errors in an ERD
questions.text: A student drew this ERD for a hospital: *Doctor M——M Patient* (no other entities); `DoctorID` is stored as a foreign key in the Doctor table. Select the **two** errors.

options.content: The M:M relationship has not been resolved with a link entity such as Appointment
Doctor and Patient should not be entities
A foreign key is placed in the table where it is the primary key
Crow's foot notation cannot show M:M

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Build an ERD: a gym
questions.text:
A gym keeps data about its **members**, **trainers** and training **sessions**. Each session is for one member with one trainer. A member has many sessions, and a trainer runs many sessions.

Draw the ERD: add one box per entity (its name on the first line), connect the entities that are related, then select each line and choose its degree. Do **not** leave a many-to-many relationship in the diagram. Draw only the entities the scenario needs.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Member, Trainer, Session (1 item each)
Relationships: Member 1:M Session; Trainer 1:M Session (1 item each, with the correct degree)
5 items in all; the 3 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Member 1 —— M Session M —— 1 Trainer
scheme.explanation: Member and Trainer are M:M; the Session entity resolves it into two 1:M relationships with the crow's feet at Session.

questions.title: Where design fits
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

Database design takes the requirements specification produced in the [[1]] stage. Its products, the ERD and the data dictionary, are used in the [[2]] stage to build the tables, and later by testers to choose test [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) analysis (2) development (3) data
scheme.explanation: Design sits between analysis (what is needed) and development (building it); the data dictionary also guides testing.

questions.title: Entity, instance, attribute
questions.text: The entity *Student* has 5 attributes, and the school has 300 students. What does this become in the database?

options.content: One table with 300 columns and 5 rows
One table with 5 columns and 300 rows
Five tables, one per attribute
300 tables, one per student

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Each attribute is a field (column) and each instance — one student — is a record (row).

questions.title: Storing a derived attribute
questions.text: A student's *Age* should be stored as an attribute next to *DateOfBirth*, so that it does not have to be calculated.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Age is a derived attribute: it can always be calculated from DateOfBirth, and a stored age would become wrong every birthday.

questions.title: Atomic attributes
questions.text: Why is a student's name usually stored as *FirstName* and *Surname* rather than one attribute *FullName*?

options.content: Two fields use less storage than one
Attributes should be atomic, so the school can sort by surname and use the first name on its own
A primary key must be made of two fields
The DBMS cannot store spaces in text fields

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: An atomic attribute holds one value that cannot sensibly be split; split names allow sorting by surname and letters such as “Dear Dana”.

questions.title: Anomalies of a poor design
questions.text:
*A music school keeps everything in one table: each lesson row repeats the student's name and parent's phone and the teacher's name and instrument.*

Match each problem to its type of anomaly.

left.text: A parent's new phone number has to be changed in 120 lesson rows, and one row is missed
A newly hired teacher cannot be recorded because they have no lessons yet
Deleting a student's only lesson also deletes the only copy of the student's details

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R3, L2–R1, L3–R2. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: All three are avoided by storing each fact once, in the table it describes, and linking the tables with keys.

questions.title: Natural, surrogate or composite key
questions.text:
For each primary key, decide what kind of key it is.

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: ISBN of a book in a bookshop
Registration number of a hire car

scheme.mark_scheme: ISBN of a book in a bookshop — Natural key (1); Auto-numbered LessonID — Surrogate key (1); StudentID + TeacherID + LessonDate + StartTime — Composite key (1); Registration number of a hire car — Natural key (1)
scheme.model_answer: ISBN of a book in a bookshop — Natural key; Auto-numbered LessonID — Surrogate key; StudentID + TeacherID + LessonDate + StartTime — Composite key; Registration number of a hire car — Natural key.
scheme.explanation: A natural key already exists in the real data; a surrogate key is an ID added by the designer; a composite key is made of two or more fields.

questions.title: Restrictions shape the design
questions.text: Match each restriction of a new system to its effect on the database design.

left.text: The school already has a licence for SQLite
The Law on Personal Data must be followed
Records will be imported from an old spreadsheet
A national register will hold 20 million people

right.text: Field types and sizes must be able to hold the old values, or the data is cleaned
Only the data types that this DBMS supports can be used
Keys must be large enough, e.g. INT rather than a two-character code
Only necessary personal fields are stored; medical notes go in a separate, protected table

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R2, L2–R4, L3–R1, L4–R3. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Each restriction must be linked to a concrete consequence — this is what a 4–6-mark “analyse” question expects.

questions.title: Teacher1, Teacher2, Teacher3
questions.text: To store Student M:M Teacher, a designer adds the fields *Teacher1*, *Teacher2* and *Teacher3* to the Student table. What is this problem called?

options.content: A repeating group
A composite key
Referential integrity
A derived attribute

scheme.mark_scheme: A.
scheme.explanation: There is never the right number of columns, many stay empty, and a search must look in three fields. The fix is a link entity.

questions.title: Keeping a 1:1 relationship
questions.text: Each student has at most one medical record and each medical record belongs to one student. Select the **two** good reasons for keeping *StudentMedical* as a separate table instead of merging it into Student.

options.content: The medical data is sensitive and can be protected with stricter access rights
A 1:1 relationship can never be merged into one table
Many students have no medical record, so the fields would often be empty in Student
A separate table removes the need for any primary key

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: A 1:1 is kept separate when the data is sensitive or when the two entities have different lives (optional records).

questions.title: Where does the dose belong?
questions.text: *A clinic: at an appointment the doctor may prescribe several medicines; each medicine is prescribed at many appointments, each time with a dose.* The M:M is resolved with the link entity **Prescription**. In which entity is the attribute *Dose* stored?

options.content: Medicine
Appointment
Prescription
Doctor

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: The dose is a fact about this medicine at this appointment — a fact about the relationship — so it belongs to the link entity.

questions.title: Circle in crow's foot notation
questions.text: At the *Lesson* end of the line Teacher — Lesson there is a small circle followed by a crow's foot. What does this show?

options.content: Exactly one lesson
One or many lessons
Zero or many lessons — a new teacher may have no lessons yet
The relationship is many-to-many

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: The circle shows optionality (“zero or…”); the crow's foot shows “many”.

questions.title: Ask in both directions
questions.text: A student knows that “one teacher gives many lessons”. Which second question decides whether Teacher — Lesson is 1:M or M:M?

options.content: Can one lesson have many teachers?
Can one teacher give no lessons?
Can one student have many lessons?
Does a lesson have a primary key?

scheme.mark_scheme: A.
scheme.explanation: The answer “no” makes it 1:M; “yes” would make it M:M. One direction alone is ambiguous.

questions.title: Build an ERD: a tour company
questions.text:
A tour company in Almaty keeps data about **customers**, **tours** and **guides**. A customer makes many **bookings**; each booking is for one customer on one tour. Each tour has many bookings. Each tour is led by one guide, and a guide leads many tours.

Draw the ERD: add one box per entity (its name on the first line), connect the entities that are related, then select each line and choose its degree. Do **not** leave a many-to-many relationship in the diagram. Draw only the entities the scenario needs.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Customer, Booking, Tour, Guide (1 item each)
Relationships: Customer 1:M Booking; Tour 1:M Booking; Guide 1:M Tour (1 item each, with the correct degree)
7 items in all; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Customer 1 —— M Booking M —— 1 Tour M —— 1 Guide
scheme.explanation: Customer M:M Tour is resolved by Booking; Guide — Tour is a plain 1:M with the crow's foot at Tour.

questions.title: Data dictionary
questions.text: Which statement best describes a **data dictionary**?

options.content: The records stored in the database
A diagram of the entities and relationships
A description of every field of every table: name, type, size, key and validation
A list of the users of the system

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: A data dictionary holds metadata — data about the data — not the records themselves.

questions.title: Items in a data dictionary
questions.text: Select **three** items recorded in a data dictionary for each field.

options.content: Data type
The value typed by the last user
Validation rule
Field size
The number of records

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Data types for Rental
questions.text: Complete the data dictionary for the table `Rental` with the most suitable data type. Use **INT**, **VARCHAR**, **DATE**, **DECIMAL**, **BOOLEAN**.

scheme.mark_scheme: RegNo VARCHAR (1); StartDate DATE (1); Days INT (1); Deposit DECIMAL (1)
scheme.model_answer: RegNo VARCHAR; StartDate DATE; Days INT; Deposit DECIMAL.
scheme.explanation: A registration number contains letters; money needs two decimal places.

questions.title: Phone number type
questions.text: Which is the most suitable data type and size for `ParentPhone` with values such as `+77015554433`?

options.content: INT
DECIMAL(12,0)
VARCHAR(12)
DATE

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: A phone number begins with + or 0 and is never used in arithmetic, so it is text; 12 characters fit +7 and 10 digits.

questions.title: Money data type
questions.text: A lesson fee is stored as values such as `12500.00`. Which data type is most suitable?

options.content: INT
DECIMAL(8,2)
VARCHAR(8)
BOOLEAN

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Money has two decimal places and is used in calculations, so DECIMAL (or REAL) is suitable; VARCHAR would stop totals being calculated.

questions.title: Matching keys
questions.text: If `CustomerID` is VARCHAR(6) in Customer, it may be INT in Rental, because it is only a foreign key there.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A foreign key must have the same data type and size as the primary key it refers to.

questions.title: Referential integrity
questions.text: Which statement describes **referential integrity**?

options.content: Every field must have a validation rule
Every foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value in the linked table
Every table must be in 3NF
Two tables may not have fields with the same name

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: E.g. a Lesson cannot refer to a student S9999 who does not exist in Student.

questions.title: Field sizes
questions.text:
Complete the data dictionary.

`StudentID` has values such as `S0107`, so its size is [[1]] characters. `ParentPhone` has values such as `+77015554433`, so its size is [[2]] characters.

scheme.explanation: Count every character, including the letter S and the + sign.

questions.title: Choose the check
questions.text: Tick (✓) the **most suitable** validation check for each field.

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Presence (1); 2 Range (1); 3 Lookup (1); 4 Format (1)
scheme.model_answer: Surname (must be filled in) — Presence; Capacity (1 to 40 seats) — Range; Instrument (piano, dombra, violin, guitar) — Lookup; StudentID (S followed by 4 digits) — Format.
scheme.explanation: A range check needs limits; a lookup check needs a short list of allowed values; a format check needs a pattern.

questions.title: From the dictionary to SQL
questions.text: Match each data dictionary entry to the SQL that implements it.

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R4, L2–R3, L3–R2, L4–R1. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Presence check in SQL
questions.text: State the SQL keyword(s) written after a field definition so that the field **cannot be left empty**.

scheme.mark_scheme: NOT NULL
scheme.explanation: NOT NULL implements a presence check.

questions.title: Order of creating tables
questions.text: Student, Teacher and Room are each related 1:M to Lesson, which holds three foreign keys. Which table must be created **last**?

options.content: Student
Teacher
Room
Lesson

scheme.mark_scheme: D.
scheme.explanation: A foreign key can only reference a table that already exists, so the link table on the "many" side is created last.

questions.title: Complete CREATE TABLE
questions.text:
Complete the SQL.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Room (
  RoomNo   INT [[1]] KEY,
  Capacity INT [[2]] (Capacity BETWEEN 1 AND 40)
);
-- in Lesson:
FOREIGN KEY (RoomNo) [[3]] Room(RoomNo)
```

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) primary (2) check (3) references

questions.title: Errors in a data dictionary
questions.text: A data dictionary contains these rows. Select the **two** rows that contain an error.

options.content: `StudentID` — VARCHAR(5) — PK — presence, unique — S0107
`ParentPhone` — INT — — — length 12 — +77015554433
`Surname` — VARCHAR(30) — — — range 1 to 100 — Seitova

scheme.mark_scheme: B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: B: a phone number with + must be VARCHAR. D: a range check does not suit a surname — use presence / length.

questions.title: Every table has a primary key
questions.text: In a well-designed database every table, including a link table such as Lesson, has a primary key.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Every table needs a field (or combination of fields) that uniquely identifies each record.

questions.title: Keys in the Lesson table
questions.text: Complete the *Key* column of the data dictionary for the table `Lesson`. Write **PK**, **FK** or **none**.

scheme.mark_scheme: LessonID Key: PK (1); TeacherID Key: FK (1); LessonDate Key: none (1)
scheme.model_answer: LessonID Key: PK; TeacherID Key: FK; LessonDate Key: none
scheme.explanation: TeacherID is the primary key of Teacher, copied into Lesson to link the tables.

questions.title: Data about the data
questions.text: A data dictionary is often called **metadata**. What does this mean?

options.content: It contains a backup copy of every record
It is data about the data: it describes the rules every record must follow, not the records themselves
It stores the data in a compressed form
It is the list of users who may open the database

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: The dictionary describes each field (type, size, validation…); the school's actual records are in the tables.

questions.title: Test data from the dictionary
questions.text:
The data dictionary says: `Capacity` — INT — range 1–40. A tester plans test data. Classify each value.

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

scheme.mark_scheme: 20 — Normal (1); 40 — Boundary (1); 1 — Boundary (1); 41 — Invalid (must be rejected) (1); ten — Invalid (must be rejected) (1)
scheme.model_answer: 20 — Normal; 40 — Boundary; 1 — Boundary; 41 — Invalid (must be rejected); ten — Invalid (must be rejected).
scheme.explanation: Normal data is well inside the range, boundary data is at the limits, and values outside the range or of the wrong type must be rejected.

questions.title: Text and number types
questions.text: Match each field to the most suitable data type.

left.text: Region code, always two letters, e.g. `KZ`
Room temperature measured by a sensor, e.g. 21.7

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R3, L2–R2, L3–R4, L4–R1. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: CHAR suits fixed-length codes, VARCHAR text of varying length, DECIMAL exact money, REAL approximate measurements.

questions.title: Dates stored as text
questions.text: A designer stores `LessonDate` as VARCHAR(10) with values such as `12/10/2026`. Select the **two** problems this causes.

options.content: The dates sort alphabetically, so 02/11/2026 comes before 12/10/2026
An impossible date such as 31/02/2026 is accepted
The DBMS cannot store the slash character
The field can no longer be part of a primary key

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: A DATE field sorts in date order, rejects impossible dates and allows calculations such as “the last 30 days”.

questions.title: Size of a price
questions.text: A bookshop stores prices up to 99 999.99 tenge. Complete the data type: `Price DECIMAL([[1]], [[2]])`.

scheme.explanation: Five digits before the point plus two after gives 7 digits in total, 2 of them decimal places.

questions.title: Which validation check?
questions.text: Match each validation rule to the name of the check.

left.text: `StudentID` must be `S` followed by four digits
`Instrument` must be piano, dombra, violin or guitar
No two students may have the same IIN

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R3, L2–R5, L3–R1, L4–R6, L5–R2, L6–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Validation or verification
questions.text:
Decide whether each method is validation or verification.

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: The computer rejects a capacity of 45 because the range is 1–40
The user types a new password twice and the two are compared
A second person checks the typed records against the paper forms
The DBMS refuses an empty lesson date

scheme.mark_scheme: The computer rejects a capacity of 45 because the range is 1–40 — Validation (1); The user types a new password twice and the two are compared — Verification (1); A second person checks the typed records against the paper forms — Verification (1); The DBMS refuses an empty lesson date — Validation (1)
scheme.model_answer: The computer rejects a capacity of 45 because the range is 1–40 — Validation; The user types a new password twice and the two are compared — Verification; A second person checks the typed records against the paper forms — Verification; The DBMS refuses an empty lesson date — Validation.
scheme.explanation: Validation is an automatic check that data is reasonable; verification checks it was entered exactly as in the source.

questions.title: What validation cannot do
questions.text: A parent's real number is `+77015554434`, but the receptionist types `+77015554433`. The field has a length check (12) and a format check (`+7` + 10 digits). What happens?

options.content: The value is rejected by the format check
The value is accepted, because validation only checks that data is sensible, not that it is correct
The value is rejected by referential integrity
The DBMS corrects the last digit automatically

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Only verification (e.g. checking against the form) could catch this error.

questions.title: Three kinds of integrity
questions.text: Match each kind of data integrity to the rule that protects it.

right.text: Every value has the right data type and size and passes its validation
Every table has a primary key that is unique and never empty
Every foreign-key value matches an existing primary-key value

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R2, L2–R3, L3–R1. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Deleting a referenced record
questions.text: Lesson has `FOREIGN KEY (StudentID) REFERENCES Student(StudentID)`. Someone tries to delete student `S0107`, who still has lessons. What does the DBMS do, and why?

options.content: Deletes the student and leaves the lessons unchanged
Refuses the delete, because the lessons would refer to a student who does not exist (referential integrity)
Deletes the student and sets every StudentID in Lesson to S0107
Refuses the delete, because StudentID is NOT NULL in Student

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Once the tables are created the DBMS enforces the rules of the design on every change, whatever program sends it.

questions.title: Validate in the form and in the database
questions.text: Good systems validate data **both** in the input form and in the database. Select the **two** correct reasons.

options.content: The form gives the user a friendly message at once
The database rule stops bad data that arrives by another route, not through the form
Validating twice makes the data correct
A format such as `S` + 4 digits can only be checked in the database

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Format checks are usually done in the form (input mask, pattern); the database's constraints protect against any route around the form.

questions.title: Create the Teacher table
questions.text:
The data dictionary of the music school contains:

| Field name | Data type | Size | Key | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TeacherID | VARCHAR | 4 | PK | Presence, unique |
| Name | VARCHAR | 50 | | Presence |
| Instrument | VARCHAR | 20 | | |

Write the SQL statement that creates the table **Teacher**.

Press **Show the database** to see the tables, **Run SQL** to try your code, then **Check Answer**.

scheme.mark_scheme: Marked by running your code on the sample database and comparing the result with a model answer.

sql.solution: CREATE TABLE Teacher (TeacherID VARCHAR(4) PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Instrument VARCHAR(20));
sql.check_query: SELECT lower(column_name) AS column_name, data_type, character_maximum_length AS size, numeric_precision, numeric_scale, is_nullable FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND lower(table_name) = 'teacher' ORDER BY ordinal_position
sql.check_label: The fields, data types and sizes are right
probes: INSERT INTO Teacher VALUES ('T012', 'Gulnara Abenova', 'piano'), ('T012', 'Yerlan Sadykov', 'dombra')

questions.title: Create the Room table with validation
questions.text:
The data dictionary of the music school contains:

| Field name | Data type | Key | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|
| RoomNo | INT | PK | Presence, unique |
| Capacity | INT | | Presence; range 1–40 |
| HasPiano | BOOLEAN | | Default False |

Write the SQL statement that creates the table **Room**, with the validation turned into `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` and `DEFAULT`.

Press **Show the database** to see the tables, **Run SQL** to try your code, then **Check Answer**.

scheme.mark_scheme: Marked by running your code on the sample database and comparing the result with a model answer.

questions.title: Designing the Sapa sports centre database
questions.text:
The **Sapa** sports centre in Shymkent is designing a database for bookings.

*Each **member** has a member number, name, phone and date of joining. Each **coach** has a coach number, name and speciality. The centre runs fitness **classes**; each class has a class code, a title, a day, a start time and a maximum size, and is led by one coach. A member can book places on many classes, and each class is booked by many members. For every **booking** the centre records the date the booking was made and whether the member attended.*

parts.title: Attribute
parts.text: Define the term **attribute**.

scheme.mark_scheme: - a single property / item of data about an entity / a field (column) of a table (1)
scheme.model_answer: An attribute is one property of an entity, e.g. a member's phone number; it becomes a field of the table.

parts.title: The Member–Class relationship
parts.text: State the degree of the relationship between **Member** and **Class**, and explain how it must be implemented in the database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- many-to-many / M:M (1)
- a field can hold only one value / a single FK cannot store many classes or many members, so it cannot be implemented directly (1)
- a link entity / table (Booking) is added with two foreign keys, giving two 1:M relationships (1)

points.criterion: Why it cannot be implemented directly
Link entity with two FKs / two 1:M

scheme.model_answer: It is M:M: a member books many classes and a class has many members. One foreign key can hold only one value, so neither table can store the link; a link table Booking with MemberNo and ClassCode as foreign keys turns it into Member 1:M Booking and Class 1:M Booking.

parts.title: Draw the ERD
parts.text: Draw the ERD for the sports centre with the entities **Member**, **Coach**, **Class** and **Booking**. Connect the related entities and give every relationship its degree. Do not leave a many-to-many relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Member, Coach, Class, Booking (1 item each)
Relationships: Coach 1:M Class; Member 1:M Booking; Class 1:M Booking (1 item each, with the correct degree)
7 items; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Coach 1 —— M Class; Member 1 —— M Booking; Class 1 —— M Booking

parts.title: Keys of Booking
parts.text: Identify a suitable **primary key** and the **foreign keys** of the table **Booking**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- primary key: BookingID / BookingNo (or the composite MemberNo + ClassCode) (1)
- foreign keys: MemberNo **and** ClassCode (both needed) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Primary key: BookingID. Foreign keys: MemberNo (→ Member) and ClassCode (→ Class).

questions.title: The data dictionary for Member
questions.text: The analyst at Sapa now writes the **data dictionary**. Example data for one member: member number `M0457`, name `Aliya Sarsenova`, phone `+77071234567`, date of joining `03/09/2026`.

parts.title: Data types and sizes
parts.text: Complete the data dictionary for the table **Member** by giving the most suitable **data type** and **size** of each field.

scheme.mark_scheme:
MemberNo: VARCHAR / text (5) (1)
Name: VARCHAR / text with a sensible size 30–60 (1)
Phone: VARCHAR / text, size 12 (1)
DateJoined: DATE (no size / 10) (1)
The type and the size must both be correct for the mark.
scheme.model_answer: MemberNo VARCHAR(5); Name VARCHAR(50); Phone VARCHAR(12); DateJoined DATE.

parts.title: Validation rules
parts.text: Suggest a suitable **validation rule** for each field. Give the rule, not only the name of the check.

scheme.mark_scheme:
MemberNo (1): format M followed by 4 digits / presence and unique
Phone (1): length 12 / format +7 followed by 10 digits
DateJoined (1): range, e.g. not after today / not before the centre opened; or format DD/MM/YYYY
Only the name of a check with no rule = 0.
scheme.model_answer: MemberNo: format M + 4 digits, unique. Phone: length 12, starts with +7. DateJoined: not later than today's date.

parts.title: Phone as text
parts.text: Explain why **Phone** should not be stored as an integer.

scheme.mark_scheme: - it starts with + (or 0) / contains symbols, which an integer cannot hold / would lose; no arithmetic is done with it (1)
scheme.model_answer: It begins with + and may begin with 0, which an integer cannot store, and nobody calculates with phone numbers.

parts.title: Why a data dictionary
parts.text: Explain **one** reason why the data dictionary is written **before** the tables are created.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- reason, e.g. programmers build every table with the same agreed names / types / sizes (1)
- consequence, e.g. so keys match and tables can be joined / fewer errors to fix after data is entered / validation is applied consistently (1)
scheme.model_answer: It gives programmers one agreed definition of every field, so the keys in different tables have the same type and size and the tables can be joined without rebuilding them later.

questions.title: Implementing the Booking table
questions.text:
The design of **Booking** in the data dictionary:

| Field | Type | Key | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|
| BookingID | INT, auto-increment | PK | unique |
| MemberNo | VARCHAR(5) | FK → Member | must exist in Member; presence |
| ClassCode | VARCHAR(6) | FK → Class | must exist in Class; presence |
| BookedOn | DATE | | presence |
| Attended | BOOLEAN | | default False |

parts.title: Referential integrity
parts.text: Explain the meaning of **referential integrity** using the field **MemberNo** in Booking as an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- every foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value in the linked table (1)
- e.g. a booking cannot have MemberNo M9999 unless member M9999 exists in Member / a member with bookings cannot simply be deleted (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every foreign key must refer to a record that exists: a Booking can only contain a MemberNo that is already in the Member table.

parts.title: Write CREATE TABLE
parts.text: Write the SQL statement to create the table **Booking** exactly as designed, including its primary key, both foreign keys, the presence checks and the default value.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- CREATE TABLE Booking ( … ); with all five fields (1)
- suitable types matching the design, MemberNo VARCHAR(5), ClassCode VARCHAR(6), DATE, BOOLEAN (1)
- BookingID … PRIMARY KEY (1)
- FOREIGN KEY (MemberNo) REFERENCES Member(MemberNo) and FOREIGN KEY (ClassCode) REFERENCES Class(ClassCode) (1)
- NOT NULL on MemberNo, ClassCode and BookedOn, and DEFAULT FALSE on Attended (1)
Ignore minor syntax slips (capitals, commas) if the meaning is clear.
scheme.model_answer:
CREATE TABLE Booking (
  BookingID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  MemberNo  VARCHAR(5) NOT NULL,
  ClassCode VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,
  BookedOn  DATE NOT NULL,
  Attended  BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  FOREIGN KEY (MemberNo)  REFERENCES Member(MemberNo),
  FOREIGN KEY (ClassCode) REFERENCES Class(ClassCode)
);

parts.title: Order of creation
parts.text: The tables Member, Coach, Class and Booking are created one by one. Explain why **Booking** must be created after Member and Class.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Booking contains foreign keys that reference Member and Class (1)
- a foreign key can only reference a table (primary key) that already exists, otherwise the statement fails (1)

points.criterion: Booking has FKs to Member and Class

scheme.model_answer: Booking's foreign keys refer to Member and Class; a foreign key can only point to a table that already exists, so those tables are created first.

parts.title: Attended
parts.text: State why **BOOLEAN** is a suitable data type for **Attended**.

scheme.mark_scheme: - it has only two possible values, true / false (yes / no) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Attendance is only yes or no, so a True/False field is enough.

questions.title: Reviewing a clinic design
questions.text:
A student designed a database for the **Densaulyq** clinic. *Each patient can have many appointments; each appointment is with one doctor; doctors have many appointments.* Part of the student's data dictionary for **Appointment**:

| Field | Type | Key | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|
| AppointmentID | INT | PK | unique |
| PatientID | INT | FK → Patient | must exist in Patient |
| DoctorName | VARCHAR(40) | | presence |
| AppDate | VARCHAR(10) | | presence |
| AppTime | TIME | | range check on the patient's surname |

In the Patient table, `PatientID` is VARCHAR(6), e.g. `P00321`.

parts.title: Errors in the design
parts.text: Identify **three** errors in this extract of the data dictionary. For each error, describe how it should be corrected.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any three errors, 1 mark for the error and 1 mark for its correction:
- PatientID is INT but the PK in Patient is VARCHAR(6) (1) → make it VARCHAR(6), the same as the PK (1)
- DoctorName stores the doctor's name in Appointment / no FK to Doctor (1) → replace it with DoctorID as a foreign key to a Doctor table (1)
- AppDate is VARCHAR (1) → use DATE so dates can be validated / sorted (1)
- AppTime validation refers to a surname / is unsuitable (1) → range check on the time, e.g. 08:00–18:00 (1)
The correction mark is only given with its error.
scheme.model_answer: 1 PatientID INT does not match VARCHAR(6) → VARCHAR(6). 2 DoctorName → DoctorID VARCHAR FK → Doctor. 3 AppDate VARCHAR → DATE (or AppTime validation → range 08:00–18:00).

parts.title: Checking a design
parts.text: Describe **two** checks the analyst should carry out on a database design **before** it is implemented.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two checks, 1 mark for naming the check and 1 for the description:
- requirements: every report / screen the client needs can be produced from the tables (2)
- normalisation: each fact stored once / tables in 3NF / no repeated data (2)
- keys: every table has a PK and every relationship has an FK on the many side (2)
- data types and validation: each type fits the data and each field has suitable validation (2)
- test data: sample records can be entered and joined correctly (2)
scheme.model_answer: Check the design against the requirements: every report the clinic asked for, such as a doctor's daily list, can be produced from the tables. Check normalisation: each fact, such as a doctor's name, is stored only once, so the tables are in 3NF.

questions.title: Tilashar language centre: entities, attributes and keys
questions.text:
The **Tilashar** language centre in Kostanay is replacing its paper registers with a database. Part of the requirements specification:

*Each **learner** has a learner number (e.g. `L0412`), first name, surname, date of birth and a phone number. Each **tutor** has a tutor code, a name and an e-mail address. The centre runs **courses**; each course has a course code (e.g. `EN-B1-07`), a language, a level, a start date and a weekly fee. Each course is taught by one tutor, and a tutor can teach several courses. A learner can enrol on several courses at the same time, and each course has many learners. For every enrolment the centre records the date of enrolment and the learner's final grade.*

parts.title: Entity and attribute
parts.text: Explain the difference between an **entity** and an **attribute**, using one example of each from the requirements above.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- an entity is a thing / person / object / event about which data is stored (with many instances) and becomes a table, e.g. Learner / Tutor / Course (1)
- an attribute is one property of an entity and becomes a field / column, e.g. Surname / DateOfBirth / WeeklyFee (1)
scheme.model_answer: An entity is a thing about which data is stored, such as Learner, and it becomes a table. An attribute is a single property of an entity, such as the learner's Surname, and it becomes a field of that table.
scheme.ai_instructions: Each mark needs both the meaning and a correct example from the scenario. An example that is not in the scenario (e.g. Student, Name) can be accepted if it clearly fits the centre.

parts.title: Not storing Age
parts.text: The manager asks for every learner's **age** to be shown on the class list. The analyst does **not** add an attribute *Age* to the entity Learner. Explain why.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- age is a derived attribute: it can be calculated from DateOfBirth (and today's date) (1)
- a stored age would become wrong / out of date (every birthday) and would have to be updated / it is the same fact stored twice (1)
scheme.model_answer: Age can be calculated at any time from DateOfBirth and today's date, so it is a derived attribute. If it were stored, it would become wrong on every learner's birthday unless someone updated it.

parts.title: Choosing the primary key of Learner
parts.text: A receptionist suggests that **Surname** should be the primary key of the table Learner. Explain why Surname is not suitable, and describe a more suitable primary key.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Surname is unsuitable — any two:
- two learners can have the same surname, so it is not unique (1)
- a surname can change (e.g. after marriage), but a key must not change (1)
- it is long / not fixed in length, and the key is copied into other tables as a foreign key (1)
Better key (max 1):
- the learner number (e.g. L0412) / an auto-numbered LearnerID, which is unique for every learner and never changes (1)
scheme.model_answer: Two learners can share the surname Akhmetova, so it does not identify a learner uniquely, and a surname can change, which a key must never do. A better key is the learner number such as L0412 (a surrogate key): it is unique, short and never changes.
scheme.ai_instructions: The third mark needs a named key and a reason (unique / never changes / short). Accept IIN as a natural key if the answer says it is unique and fixed.

questions.title: Tilashar: relationships and the ERD
questions.text: Use the requirements of the Tilashar language centre from question 1.

parts.title: Degrees of relationships
parts.text: State the degree of each relationship as it is described in the requirements. Write 1:1, 1:M or M:M.

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 Tutor — Course: 1:M (1)
2 Learner — Course: M:M (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1: 1:M (one tutor teaches many courses); 2: M:M (a learner takes many courses and a course has many learners).

parts.title: Resolving the M:M relationship
parts.text: Explain why the relationship between **Learner** and **Course** cannot be stored directly in a relational database, and how the analyst should resolve it.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a field can hold only one value, so neither table can store one foreign key for its many partners / extra columns Course1, Course2 … would be a repeating group (1)
- add a link entity (e.g. Enrolment) that holds the primary keys of Learner and Course as foreign keys, giving two 1:M relationships (1)

points.criterion: Why it cannot be stored directly
Link entity with both keys as FKs

scheme.model_answer: A field can hold only one value, so Learner cannot have one CourseCode field for all its courses (and Course cannot hold all its learners). A link entity Enrolment is added; each enrolment holds one LearnerNo and one CourseCode as foreign keys, so Learner 1:M Enrolment and Course 1:M Enrolment.
scheme.ai_instructions: 'Because it is M:M' alone gets no mark — the answer must say why one field cannot store many values (or describe the repeating group).

parts.title: Draw the ERD
parts.text: Draw the ERD for the language centre with the entities **Tutor**, **Course**, **Learner** and **Enrolment**. Connect the related entities and give every relationship its degree. Do not leave a many-to-many relationship in the diagram.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Tutor, Course, Learner, Enrolment (1 item each)
Relationships: Tutor 1:M Course; Course 1:M Enrolment; Learner 1:M Enrolment (1 item each, with the correct degree)
7 items; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Tutor 1 —— M Course; Course 1 —— M Enrolment; Learner 1 —— M Enrolment

parts.title: Where the final grade belongs
parts.text: The analyst must decide in which entity to store the attribute **FinalGrade**. Identify the entity and explain your choice.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Enrolment (1)
- the grade is a fact about one learner on one particular course / the relationship, not about the learner in general (who has many grades) or the course in general (which has many learners) (1)

points.criterion: Reason: fact about this learner on this course

scheme.model_answer: Enrolment. A final grade belongs to one learner on one course: a learner on three courses has three grades, and a course has a different grade for each learner, so it can only be stored once per enrolment.

questions.title: Why Tilashar needs a database design
questions.text: At the moment the centre keeps **one spreadsheet**. Each row is one enrolment and contains the learner's name and phone number, the course code, the tutor's name and e-mail address, the weekly fee and the enrolment date. A learner on three courses appears in three rows.

parts.title: Problems of the single table
parts.text: Describe **two** problems (anomalies) that storing the data in this one spreadsheet can cause. Use examples from the centre.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two of the following, 2 marks each — name / idea (1) + example from the centre (1):
- update anomaly: the learner's phone (or tutor's e-mail) is repeated in many rows, so a change must be made in every row; if one row is missed the data is inconsistent (1+1)
- insertion anomaly: a new tutor (or a new course) with no enrolments yet cannot be recorded, because every row must be an enrolment (1+1)
- deletion anomaly: deleting a learner's only enrolment also deletes the only copy of the learner's details (1+1)
- data redundancy: the same details are typed many times, wasting storage / time and causing typing errors (1+1) — max once
scheme.model_answer: Update anomaly: a learner on three courses has her phone number in three rows; if she changes it and only one row is edited, the centre has two different numbers. Insertion anomaly: a newly hired tutor who has no course yet cannot be entered, because every row has to be an enrolment.

parts.title: Restrictions of the new system
parts.text: Before drawing the ERD the analyst lists the **restrictions** of the new system. Explain how **two** different restrictions could affect the design of the Tilashar database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two restrictions, 2 marks each — restriction (1) + consequence for the design (1), e.g.:
- legal: the Law on Personal Data — store only personal data that is needed / with consent; sensitive data in a separate table with restricted access (1+1)
- the chosen DBMS — decides which data types exist (e.g. no DATE / BOOLEAN in SQLite) and limits (1+1)
- volume of data / number of users — key types and sizes must be large enough for all future records, e.g. INT key not a 2-digit code (1+1)
- existing data imported from the spreadsheet — field types and sizes must hold the old values or the data must be cleaned (1+1)
- time and budget — a simpler design with fewer tables that still meets the requirements (1+1)
scheme.model_answer: The Law on Personal Data means the centre may store only the personal data it needs, so the analyst leaves out fields such as home address and protects the phone numbers with access rights. The data must also be imported from the old spreadsheet, so every field must be large enough to hold the old values, e.g. surnames up to 30 characters.
scheme.ai_instructions: The consequence must be a concrete effect on the database (tables, fields, types, sizes, keys, access); a general statement such as 'the design must follow the law' gets the first mark only.

questions.title: The data dictionary for Course
questions.text:
The analyst writes the **data dictionary** for the table **Course**. Example data for one course:

| CourseCode | Language | Level | StartDate | WeeklyFee | MaxLearners | Online |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EN-B1-07 | English | B1 | 14/01/2027 | 8500.00 | 12 | Yes |

Levels are always one of A1, A2, B1, B2 or C1. A group never has more than 15 learners. The weekly fee is never more than 50 000 tenge.

parts.title: Data types and sizes
parts.text: Complete the data dictionary by giving the most suitable **data type** and **size** of each field. Write — if no size is needed.

scheme.mark_scheme:
CourseCode: VARCHAR / CHAR / text, size 8 (1)
StartDate: DATE, no size (accept 10 if the type is DATE) (1)
WeeklyFee: DECIMAL / currency with 2 decimal places, e.g. DECIMAL(7,2) / (8,2) (1)
Online: BOOLEAN / Yes-No, no size (1)
The type and the size must both be correct for the mark; INT or REAL / FLOAT for WeeklyFee = 0.
scheme.model_answer: CourseCode VARCHAR(8); StartDate DATE (—); WeeklyFee DECIMAL(7,2); Online BOOLEAN (—).

parts.title: Validation rules
parts.text: Suggest a suitable **validation rule** for each field. Give the rule with its values or limits, not only the name of the check.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Level (1): lookup / list check — must be one of A1, A2, B1, B2, C1
MaxLearners (1): range check 1–15 (accept 1 ≤ x ≤ 15; type whole number with the range)
CourseCode (1): format two letters, dash, level, dash, two digits (e.g. LL-XX-99) / length exactly 8 / presence and unique
Only the name of a check with no rule = 0.
scheme.model_answer: Level: lookup — one of A1, A2, B1, B2, C1. MaxLearners: range 1 to 15. CourseCode: format two capital letters, '-', level, '-', two digits; unique and not empty.

parts.title: Validation and verification
parts.text: A receptionist enters **MaxLearners** as **11** instead of **12**. The validation rule does not reject it. Explain why, and state a method that **could** detect this error.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- validation only checks that data is reasonable / follows the rule; 11 is inside the allowed range, so it is accepted (1)
- verification, e.g. double entry / a second person checks the entry against the source document (visual check) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Validation only checks that the value is sensible, and 11 is within the range 1–15, so it passes. Verification would detect it — for example, a visual check of the entered data against the course form, or typing the value twice.

questions.title: Building the Enrolment table
questions.text:
The data dictionary for the link table **Enrolment**:

| Field | Type | Key | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|
| EnrolID | INT, auto-increment | PK | unique |
| LearnerNo | CHAR(5) | FK → Learner | must exist in Learner; presence |
| CourseCode | VARCHAR(8) | FK → Course | must exist in Course; presence |
| EnrolDate | DATE | | presence |
| FinalGrade | INT | | range 0–100 |

parts.title: Write CREATE TABLE
parts.text: Write the SQL statement to create the table **Enrolment** exactly as designed, including the primary key, both foreign keys, the presence checks and the range check.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- CREATE TABLE Enrolment ( … ); with all five fields and the types from the design (1)
- EnrolID … PRIMARY KEY (1)
- FOREIGN KEY (LearnerNo) REFERENCES Learner(LearnerNo) and FOREIGN KEY (CourseCode) REFERENCES Course(CourseCode) (1)
- NOT NULL on LearnerNo, CourseCode and EnrolDate and CHECK (FinalGrade BETWEEN 0 AND 100) / >= 0 AND <= 100 (1)
Ignore minor syntax slips (capitals, commas) if the meaning is clear.

points.criterion: CREATE TABLE with all fields and types

scheme.model_answer:
CREATE TABLE Enrolment (
  EnrolID    INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  LearnerNo  CHAR(5)    NOT NULL,
  CourseCode VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
  EnrolDate  DATE       NOT NULL,
  FinalGrade INT CHECK (FinalGrade BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
  FOREIGN KEY (LearnerNo)  REFERENCES Learner(LearnerNo),
  FOREIGN KEY (CourseCode) REFERENCES Course(CourseCode)
);

parts.title: Deleting a learner
parts.text: After the tables are created, the receptionist tries to delete learner **L0412**, who still has two enrolments. Explain what the DBMS does and why.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the DBMS refuses / rejects the deletion (unless the enrolments are deleted first) (1)
- the two Enrolment records would have a LearnerNo that matches no learner; the foreign key constraint enforces referential integrity (1)

points.criterion: Reason: referential integrity / FK would point to nothing

scheme.model_answer: The DBMS refuses to delete the learner. Two Enrolment records still contain LearnerNo L0412 as a foreign key; deleting the learner would leave them pointing at a learner who does not exist, which breaks referential integrity.

summary: Designing the database for a new system — finding entities and attributes in the requirements, deciding the degree of each relationship, drawing the ERD and resolving many-to-many relationships, then writing a complete data dictionary (data types, sizes, keys, validation) for every table and turning the design into CREATE TABLE statements.

theory.title: Database design in the system life cycle

blocks.content: During the **design** stage of a new system the analyst turns the **requirements specification** into an exact plan of the database. Nothing is built yet: the plan is checked with the client first, because a mistake found on paper costs minutes, but a mistake found after the tables are full of data costs days.

blocks.text: Where database design fits in the life cycle

blocks.content: Database design sits between **analysis** and **development**. In the analysis stage the analyst interviewed the users, observed the current system and collected its documents, and the result was a **requirements specification**: a list of what the new system must store, what it must let users do and which reports it must produce. Database design takes that list and answers a different question — not *what* is needed, but *how exactly the data will be organised* so that every requirement can be met. The output of design is then the input of development: a programmer opens the ERD and the data dictionary and builds the tables in the chosen DBMS (for example MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite or Microsoft Access) without having to guess anything.

The design is also used **after** development. Testers read the data dictionary to choose **test data** — a valid value, a boundary value and an invalid value for every validated field — and to check that invalid data really is rejected. Years later, when the system is maintained or extended, a new programmer reads the same documents to understand the database before changing it. This is why the ERD and the data dictionary are kept as part of the **technical documentation** of the system, not thrown away once the tables exist.
A database is never designed in a vacuum. Before drawing anything the analyst must analyse the **restrictions (constraints)** of the new system, because each one changes the design:

items: **The DBMS and hardware.** The chosen DBMS decides which data types exist (SQLite has no true BOOLEAN or DATE type; MySQL has both) and how large a table can become. A school that already has a licence for one product will not buy another.

**Volume of data and number of users.** A library of 3 000 books and a national register of 20 million people need very different decisions about key sizes, indexes and performance. An `INT` key is enough for millions of records; a two-digit `VARCHAR(2)` key would run out after 100.

**Legal restrictions.** In Kazakhstan the Law on Personal Data and its Protection requires that personal data (names, IIN, phone numbers, health data) is collected only with consent, stored securely and kept only as long as needed. The design must therefore decide which personal fields are really necessary, and may put sensitive data (e.g. medical notes) in a separate table with stricter access rights.
**Time and budget.** A small project may use a simpler design with fewer tables if it still meets every requirement; there is no reason to model data that nobody will ever ask for.
**Existing data.** If records are imported from an old spreadsheet, the new field types and sizes must be able to hold the old values — or the data must be cleaned during conversion.

blocks.content: Writing these restrictions down explains *why* the design looks the way it does, and in an exam a 4–6-mark "analyse" question about a new system expects you to link each restriction to a concrete consequence for the database.

blocks.text: Why a poor design causes problems

blocks.content: Imagine the music school stores everything in **one** big table: every lesson row repeats the student's name and phone number and the teacher's name and instrument. It looks simple, but it causes three kinds of **anomaly**:

items: **Update anomaly.** A parent changes their phone number. The number is stored in all 120 lesson rows of their child, so all 120 must be changed; if one is missed, the database now contains two different numbers and nobody knows which is right.
**Insertion anomaly.** A new teacher is hired but has no lessons yet. There is no lesson row to put them in, so the teacher cannot be recorded at all.
**Deletion anomaly.** A student's only lesson is deleted, and with it the only copy of the student's details.

blocks.content: A good design avoids all three by storing **each fact once**, in the table about the thing it describes (the phone number in *Student*, the instrument in *Teacher*), and by linking tables through **keys** instead of copying data. This is exactly what the ERD and the data dictionary make visible before a single record is typed in.

The stage of system design in which the analyst decides **which tables (entities)** the database will have, **which fields (attributes)** each table holds, **how the tables are related**, and the **data type, size, key and validation** of every field. Its products are the **ERD** and the **data dictionary**.
A **thing (person, object, event) about which data is stored**, with many instances — e.g. *Student*, *Teacher*, *Lesson*. Each entity becomes **one table**.
A **single property of an entity** — e.g. *Surname*, *DateOfBirth*. Each attribute becomes **one field (column)** of the table.
A **link between two entities**, e.g. *a teacher teaches many lessons*. Its **degree** is one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:M) or many-to-many (M:M). In the database it is made with a **foreign key**.

A **primary key (PK)** is a field that **uniquely identifies each record** of a table (e.g. `StudentID`). A **foreign key (FK)** is a field in one table that is the **primary key of another table**, used to **link** the two tables.

items.title: Why design the database first
items.content:
- Errors are found **on paper**, before data is entered.
- The client can **check** that every report they need can be produced.
- Several programmers build tables that **fit together** (same keys and types).
- The design becomes part of the **technical documentation** for maintenance.

items.title: What a good design achieves
items.content:
- Each fact is stored **once** — no data redundancy (tables in 3NF).
- Every table has a **primary key**; every relationship has a **foreign key**.
- Every field has a **suitable data type** and **validation**, so data integrity is high.
- The database can be **extended** later without rebuilding it.

blocks.title: Worked example — the Aqkuy music school
blocks.content:
*The Aqkuy music school in Almaty wants a system to manage lessons. Each **student** has an ID, first name, surname, date of birth and a parent's phone number. Each **teacher** has an ID, a name and the instrument they teach. Every week a student has individual **lessons**, possibly with several different teachers; for each lesson the school records the date, the start time, the room and whether the student attended. Each **room** has a number and a capacity.*

1. **Underline the nouns:** student, ID, name, date of birth, phone, teacher, instrument, lesson, date, time, room, number, capacity.
2. **Keep the nouns with their own data and many instances:** Student, Teacher, Lesson, Room → **entities**.
3. **The other nouns describe an entity:** name, date of birth, instrument, capacity… → **attributes**.
4. **Give each entity a primary key:** StudentID, TeacherID, LessonID, RoomNo.

| Entity | Attributes (PK underlined in the ERD) |
|---|---|
| Student | **StudentID**, FirstName, Surname, DateOfBirth, ParentPhone |
| Teacher | **TeacherID**, Name, Instrument |
| Room | **RoomNo**, Capacity |
| Lesson | **LessonID**, LessonDate, StartTime, Attended (+ foreign keys added in step 2) |

rows: Yes — a Teacher has an ID, a name, an instrument
No — an instrument is just one value

blocks.text: Entity, instance and attribute — getting the level right

blocks.content: It helps to separate three ideas. An **entity** is the *kind* of thing — *Student*. An **instance** (or occurrence) of the entity is one particular student — Dana Seitova, S0107 — and becomes one **record (row)** in the table. An **attribute** is one property that every instance has — *DateOfBirth* — and becomes one **field (column)**. So the entity *Student* with five attributes and 300 instances becomes a table with five columns and 300 rows. If you can only think of **one** instance of something (the school itself, "the director"), it is usually not an entity at all but a fixed setting of the system.

Two further rules decide which attributes to keep. First, attributes should be **atomic** — one value that cannot sensibly be split. *FullName* is better stored as *FirstName* and *Surname*, because the school will want to sort by surname and write letters "Dear Dana"; an address is often split into *Street*, *City* and *PostCode* for the same reason. Second, **derived** attributes are normally **not stored**. A student's *Age* can always be calculated from *DateOfBirth* and today's date; if *Age* were stored it would be wrong one day a year. Likewise a lesson's *TotalFee* is calculated from the price and the number of lessons, not typed in.

Every entity needs a **primary key** so that each instance can be found and referred to without confusion. Sometimes the scenario already contains a field that is unique and stable — a **natural key**, such as a car's registration number or a book's ISBN. Often it does not: names repeat, phone numbers change and e-mail addresses are given up. Then the designer adds a **surrogate key** — an ID with no meaning of its own, such as `StudentID` or an auto-numbered `LessonID`. Surrogate keys are short, never change and never repeat, which makes them ideal for copying into other tables as foreign keys.

A key can also be **composite** — made of two or more fields together. In a link entity such as *Lesson*, the combination *StudentID + TeacherID + LessonDate + StartTime* identifies a lesson uniquely, so it could be the key. In practice designers usually add a single surrogate key (`LessonID`) because a one-field key is easier to refer to, and they keep the combination unique with a separate rule.

blocks.title: How to choose a primary key
items: Use a field that is **unique** for every record and **never empty** — e.g. a student number.
If no natural field is unique (names repeat!), **create an ID** field, often auto-incremented.
The key should **not change** over time — not a phone number or a surname.
Keep it **short** and simple, because it is copied into other tables as a foreign key.

blocks.content:
- Making a **single value** an entity — "Date" or "Instrument" are attributes, not tables.
- Choosing **Name** as a primary key — two students can have the same name.
- Forgetting the **event** entities: *Lesson*, *Loan*, *Rental*, *Order* are entities too, not only people and objects.
- Putting the same attribute (e.g. the teacher's name) into **several** entities — store it once.
For every pair of entities that are related, ask the question **in both directions**: "Can one A have many B?" and "Can one B have many A?". The two answers give the **degree** of the relationship.

Why both directions? Because one answer alone is ambiguous. "One teacher gives many lessons" is true for a 1:M relationship *and* for an M:M one; only the reverse question — "can one lesson have many teachers?" — tells them apart. Always answer the questions **for the scenario you are given**, not for the real world in general: in a music school with individual lessons, a lesson has one student; in a school with group lessons the same pair would be M:M and would need another link entity (*Enrolment*).

**One-to-many (1:M)** is by far the most common relationship and the one a relational database stores most naturally. One record on the "one" side (a teacher) is linked to any number of records on the "many" side (lessons), but each "many" record belongs to exactly one "one" record. It is implemented by putting the **primary key of the "one" table into the "many" table as a foreign key**: each lesson row has a `TeacherID` column. The foreign key must go on the "many" side because each lesson has *one* teacher — one value that fits in one field — while a teacher has *many* lessons, which would never fit in one field.

**One-to-one (1:1)** is rare. One instance of A is linked to at most one instance of B and vice versa — for example, each teacher is in charge of one classroom and each classroom has one teacher in charge. A 1:1 relationship can often be merged into one table; it is kept separate when the two entities have different lives (classrooms exist without a teacher in charge) or when some of the data is sensitive and must be protected separately (a *StudentMedical* table linked 1:1 to *Student*). The foreign key can go in either table, usually in the one whose records are optional.

**Many-to-many (M:M)** means that both questions get the answer "yes": a student has many teachers and a teacher has many students. Relational databases **cannot store an M:M relationship directly**. Try it: if `TeacherID` is put in *Student*, each student can have only one teacher. If columns *Teacher1*, *Teacher2*, *Teacher3* are added, the table has a **repeating group** — there is never the right number of columns, most of them are empty, and searching "all students of T012" means searching three columns. Putting `StudentID` in *Teacher* fails in the same way. The solution is a **link entity** (also called a junction or associative entity) between them, whose every record links **one** student to **one** teacher. The M:M is then replaced by two 1:M relationships, each with its foreign key in the link entity.

An entity added to **resolve a many-to-many relationship**: it sits between the two entities, is on the **"many" side of two 1:M relationships**, and holds the **primary keys of both as foreign keys** — e.g. *Lesson* between *Student* and *Teacher*, *Loan* between *Member* and *Book*.

blocks.caption: Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link entity

blocks.content: An ERD is only useful if everyone reads it the same way, so a standard notation is used. In **crow's foot notation** each entity is a box with its name at the top (and, in a detailed ERD, its attributes, with the PK and FKs marked). A line joins two related entities, and the symbol at **each end** describes how many instances of *that* entity can be linked to one instance of the entity at the other end: a **single bar** means "one", a **crow's foot** (three prongs) means "many". To read a relationship, start at one box, follow the line and read the symbol at the far end: "one **Teacher** … teaches … **many** (crow's foot) Lessons"; then go back the other way: "one **Lesson** … is taught by … **one** (bar) Teacher".

Some textbooks and exam papers also mark **optionality** with a small circle ("zero or …"): a teacher who has just been hired may have **zero** lessons, so the Lesson end could show circle + crow's foot ("zero or many"). At this level you are mainly assessed on the **degree**, but if the scenario says "every lesson *must* have a teacher" you can show the single bar as "exactly one". Whatever notation is used, labels like `1` and `M` written next to the ends are always acceptable in an exam and remove any doubt.

blocks.title: Worked example — an ERD for the Shipager clinic
blocks.content:
*A private clinic in Shymkent records patients (IIN, name, phone), doctors (ID, name, speciality) and appointments (date, time, room, notes). Each appointment is for one patient with one doctor. At an appointment the doctor may prescribe several medicines; each medicine (code, name, price) is prescribed at many appointments, with a dose.*

1. **Entities:** Patient, Doctor, Appointment, Medicine.
2. **Patient — Appointment:** a patient has many appointments; an appointment is for one patient → **1:M**, FK `PatientIIN` in Appointment.
3. **Doctor — Appointment:** a doctor has many appointments; an appointment has one doctor → **1:M**, FK `DoctorID` in Appointment.
4. **Appointment — Medicine:** one appointment → many medicines, and one medicine → many appointments → **M:M**. Resolve it with the link entity **Prescription** (`AppointmentID` FK, `MedicineCode` FK, `Dose`). The *Dose* belongs here: it is not a fact about the medicine in general, nor about the appointment in general, but about *this medicine at this appointment*.
5. **Final ERD:** Patient 1:M Appointment M:1 Doctor; Appointment 1:M Prescription M:1 Medicine — five lines of reasoning, four 1:M relationships, no M:M left.

blocks.title: Drawing the ERD
items: Draw **one box per entity**, named in the singular (Student, not Students) — or plural everywhere, but be consistent.
Write the attributes in the box and mark the **PK**; add the **FKs** to the tables on the "many" side.
Join every pair of **related** entities with **one line** — not every pair is related.
Show the degree at **both ends**: `1` / single bar on the "one" side, `M` / crow's foot on the "many" side.
Label the line with a verb if it helps: *teaches*, *attends*.
Replace every **M:M** with a **link entity** that has two 1:M relationships.
Check: every table has a PK, every relationship has an FK, no fact is stored twice (3NF).

blocks.title: Worked example — resolving M:M in a school library
blocks.content:
*Members borrow many books; over a year each book is borrowed by many members.*
- Member — Book is **M:M**, so it cannot be stored directly.
- Add the link entity **Loan** (one record per borrowing) with `LoanID` (PK), `MemberID` (FK), `BookID` (FK), `LoanDate`, `ReturnDate`.
- Now **Member 1:M Loan** and **Book 1:M Loan**. The dates belong to the **Loan**, not to the member or the book — the link entity is also the right place for facts about the relationship.

- Leaving an **M:M** line in the final ERD — always resolve it with a link entity.
- Putting the foreign key on the **"one" side** (TeacherID in Teacher is a PK; the FK belongs in Lesson).
- Drawing a crow's foot at the wrong end — the crow's foot touches the entity that has **many** records per one record of the other.
- Asking the question in **one direction only** — "a student has many lessons" alone does not tell you whether it is 1:M or M:M.
- Linking every entity to every other one — draw a line only where the scenario describes a relationship.

theory.title: Exam practice: entities, relationships and the ERD

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term entity. [1]**
A thing / object / person / event about which data is stored (and which becomes a table in the database) (1).

**Q: A gym records members, trainers and training sessions. Each session is for one member with one trainer. Identify the entities and the degree of each relationship. [4]**
Entities: Member, Trainer, Session (1). Member — Session **1:M** (1). Trainer — Session **1:M** (1). Member — Trainer is M:M, resolved by **Session** (the link entity) (1).

**Q: Explain why a many-to-many relationship cannot be implemented directly in a relational database. [2]**
A field can hold only **one value** (1), so neither table can hold a single foreign key for its **many** partners; a **link table** with two foreign keys is needed (1).

**Q: State where the foreign key is placed in a one-to-many relationship. [1]**
In the table on the **"many"** side (1).

**Q: Draw the ERD for: one customer places many orders; an order contains many products. [4]**
Entities Customer, Order, Product + link entity OrderLine (1); Customer 1:M Order (1); Order 1:M OrderLine (1); Product 1:M OrderLine (1).

**Q: A clinic stores the doctor's name and phone number in every appointment record. Explain one problem this causes. [2]**
The doctor's details are repeated in many records (data redundancy) (1); if the phone number changes it must be updated in every appointment, and a missed record leaves inconsistent data (update anomaly) (1).

**Q: Explain how one restriction of a new system can affect the database design. [2]**
E.g. the Law on Personal Data requires personal data to be protected (1), so sensitive fields such as medical notes are kept in a separate table with restricted access / only necessary fields are stored (1).

- Writing the degree as words without saying **which entity is on the "many" side**.
- Naming the link entity vaguely ("Link", "Table3") — use a meaningful name: *Lesson*, *Loan*, *OrderLine*.
- Forgetting to give marks-worthy detail: "because it is M:M" is not an explanation — say **why** one field cannot store many values.

blocks.content: When the ERD is agreed, every entity is described **field by field** in the **data dictionary**. This is the document programmers follow to create the tables, so it must be **complete and exact**.

blocks.text: What a data dictionary is for

blocks.content: The ERD shows the *shape* of the database — which tables exist and how they are linked — but it says nothing about what a value looks like. Is `TeacherID` a number or text? How long can a surname be? What happens if someone types a start time of 25:00? The **data dictionary** answers these questions. It is often described as **"data about the data" (metadata)**: it does not contain the school's records, it describes the rules every record must follow.

Because it is so exact, the data dictionary serves several people at once. **Programmers** build each table directly from it, and when several programmers work on different parts of the system they all use the same names, types and sizes, so their parts fit together. **Testers** use the validation column to plan test data: for `Capacity` with a range of 1–40 they test 20 (normal), 1 and 40 (boundary), 0 and 41 (just outside) and "ten" (wrong type). The **client** can check that the information they need is really stored. And during **maintenance** it is the first document a new developer reads. A data dictionary that leaves cells empty or says "number" instead of a real data type fails all of these people.

blocks.text: The columns of a data dictionary, one by one

blocks.content: Each **row** of the data dictionary describes one **field**, and each **column** records one fact about it:

items: **Field name** — the exact name used in the DBMS and in SQL. It should be meaningful and contain **no spaces** (`DateOfBirth` or `date_of_birth`, not `Date of birth`), and the same name should be used for a foreign key as for the primary key it refers to, so the link is obvious.

**Data type** — the kind of value stored: `INT`, `DECIMAL`, `VARCHAR`, `CHAR`, `DATE`, `TIME`, `BOOLEAN`. The type decides what the DBMS will accept and what can be done with the value (arithmetic on numbers, date comparisons on dates).

**Size / length** — for text, the maximum number of characters (`VARCHAR(30)`); for decimals, the total digits and the decimal places (`DECIMAL(8,2)`). It must fit the **longest** real value and no more, so storage is not wasted.
**Format** — how the value is written: `DD/MM/YYYY`, `S` followed by 4 digits, `+7` followed by 10 digits.
**Key** — `PK`, `FK → Table`, or blank. A field can be both part of a key and validated.
**Validation** — the rule a value must pass to be accepted, with its **limits**: "range 1–40", not just "range check".
**Description** — what the field means in the real world and why it is stored, e.g. "Parent's mobile number, used for SMS reminders".
**Example** — one realistic value. The example is a quick self-check: if the example `S0107` cannot be stored in the type you wrote, the type is wrong.

blocks.content: Some data dictionaries also include **Required (Y/N)** and **Default value** columns; both are useful and turn directly into SQL (`NOT NULL`, `DEFAULT`).

A document / table that describes **every field of every table** in the database — its **name, data type, size, format, key, validation rule, description** and an **example** value (data about the data — metadata).
The rule that **every foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value** in the linked table — e.g. a Lesson cannot refer to a student `S9999` who does not exist.
